summary: This StudySmarter explanation summarizes Adam Smith's role in founding modern economic thought and market capitalism, describing him as the father of modern capitalism. It covers his biography (baptism, Glasgow professorship, Theory of Moral Sentiments, The Wealth of Nations) and his core ideas: competitive markets and comparative advantage, the 'invisible hand', and free trade as a challenge to mercantilism. The note ends by linking his focus on production to the later development of GDP as a measure of national wealth.
one_line: Overview of Adam Smith's life and his ideas on competitive markets, the invisible hand, and free trade versus mercantilism.
key_facts: Adam Smith was a Scottish economist and philosopher, often considered the father of modern capitalism.
Adam Smith was baptized on June 5, 1723; his exact birthdate is unknown.
Smith studied at both the University of Glasgow and Oxford.
Smith was appointed professor and chair of logic and moral philosophy at the University of Glasgow in 1752.
Smith published The Theory of Moral Sentiments in 1759, which addressed sympathy and empathy and built on and challenged the work of David Hume.
Smith moved to France in 1763 and worked for a time as tutor to the stepson of Charles Townshend.
In France, Smith got to know Hume, Voltaire, and Benjamin Franklin.
Smith published The Wealth of Nations in 1776, his most well-known work, which closely associated him with capitalism.
Smith coined the concept of the 'invisible hand' of the market, which guides individuals pursuing their own economic self-interest to improve society.
Smith's theory of competitive capitalism held that individuals engaging in activities where they have a comparative advantage would benefit themselves and produce the best overall outcome.
Smith argued for a minimalist government with limited intervention in the economy, challenging mercantilism.
Mercantilism is the economic theory that exports should be maximized to produce a balance of trade in favor of the country, and it was the predominant model of European empires.
Smith argued that overall labor and production, not accumulated gold and silver, was the better measure of a nation's wealth.
Smith's focus on production contributed to the theoretical foundation of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), though Smith did not invent this measure.
